questions.q: What does where do in a KQL query?
options: Adds a new computed column
Filters rows, exactly like Foundations' .filter() or T-SQL's WHERE clause
Limits the number of rows returned
Selects which columns to keep
questions.explain: and/or combine conditions, and multiple where steps in sequence behave like one combined and condition.

questions.q: What does project combine into one operator?
options: where and take
extend and summarize
select() and alias() — naming columns to keep, with optional inline renaming
join and union
questions.explain: Columns not listed are dropped, same as a Foundations select() naming only some columns.

questions.q: How does extend differ from project?
options: extend adds a new computed column while keeping every existing column; project keeps only what's explicitly named
They do exactly the same thing
extend removes columns; project adds them
extend can only be used with the where operator
questions.explain: extend is the real KQL equivalent of Foundations Lesson 46's withColumn().

questions.q: Why would you use extend before project rather than the reverse, when both a new column and a narrower column list are needed?
options: project must always come first in every KQL query
extend needs the original columns present to compute the new one; project would have already dropped anything not explicitly kept
Order never matters in KQL, since it works like T-SQL
extend cannot be used together with project in the same query
questions.explain: This is a direct consequence of KQL's pipe-order semantics from Lesson 22.

questions.q: What does a chain like where -> extend -> project -> take accomplish?
options: It's invalid KQL syntax; only one operator can be used per query
It only performs filtering, ignoring the other three operators
Real filtering, a real computed column, a real column selection, and a real row limit — the same shape as chaining PySpark's .filter().withColumn().select().limit()
It requires a separate query for each operator
questions.explain: This mirrors a familiar PySpark transformation chain, just written with pipes instead of method dots.
